source: Metcalfe & Wiebe (1987) Intuition in insight and noninsight problem solving, Memory & Cognition 15(3)
finding: Experiment 1 (warmth ratings). Subjects rated how close they felt to the answer every 15 sec while solving 5 classic insight problems and 5 multistep (noninsight) problems. Warmth rose more gradually before correct solutions on noninsight problems than on insight problems, where it stayed low and jumped at the end.
numbers: Exp 1: 26 paid volunteers, only 19 usable (others solved nothing or solved instantly on one problem type). 3-cm visual analogue scale, up to 40 ratings per problem. Gamma between problem type and incrementalness: angular warmth G=.26, t(18)=2.02; differential warmth G=.23, t(18)=1.63 (one-tailed).
limits: Small N, modest effect, second measure only one-tailed. Only correctly solved problems are analysed. Problem labels (insight vs noninsight) were chosen by the authors, who admit their insight criterion was not well defined.
agent_relevance: The original evidence that insight is sudden to the solver. It is evidence about what people report, not about the process. Warmth is a human self-report; our agent should not copy it as a signal.

source: Metcalfe & Wiebe (1987) Intuition in insight and noninsight problem solving, Memory & Cognition 15(3)
finding: Experiment 2 (algebra versus insight). Same warmth method with algebra problems as the noninsight class. Algebra problems showed incremental warmth; insight problems showed little rise until solution.
numbers: Exp 2: 73 UBC students; 21 failed to solve at least one insight and one algebra problem (and 4 solved all algebra), leaving 48 usable for feeling-of-knowing and 39 for warmth. Warmth gamma between problem type and incrementalness: G=.35 (t(37)=3.10) and G=.32 (t(37)=2.56) for the two measures.
limits: Selection rule (must solve at least one of each type and miss at least one) removes about 34 percent of the sample for FOK and 47 percent for warmth. Algebra versus insight differ in many ways besides insight.
agent_relevance: Shows the signature a detector could look for: flat, then a step. Our impasse detector uses observable no-progress counts, not a felt rating.

source: Metcalfe & Wiebe (1987) Intuition in insight and noninsight problem solving, Memory & Cognition 15(3)
finding: Feeling of knowing did not predict who would solve an insight problem, but did predict algebra. Subjects ranked 5 unsolved problems by how likely they were to solve them, then solved them.
numbers: Rank-based FOK gamma with actual success: algebra mean G=.40, insight mean G=.08, F(1,46)=6.46; insight not above zero (t(46)=.8). Probability estimates: algebra G=.40, insight G=.15, F(1,42)=2.8 (one-tailed); insight not above zero, t(42)=1.2. The authors say the zero insight result replicates Metcalfe (1986a).
limits: Non-significant insight gamma at N=44 to 48 is not proof of no relation. Interaction one-tailed for probability estimates.
agent_relevance: Core fact for the guardrail: a solver's prediction of whether it will solve an insight-type problem carries almost no signal. Do not route on the model's stated confidence about unsolved hard problems.

source: Metcalfe & Wiebe (1987) Intuition in insight and noninsight problem solving, Memory & Cognition 15(3)
finding: People overestimated how well they would do, more on insight problems. Calibration of predicted versus actual success.
numbers: Insight: predicted .59, actual .34. Algebra: predicted .73, actual .55. Interaction F(1,46)=3.18, one-tailed only, called fairly weak by the authors.
limits: Weak interaction; overestimation is present for both types. The authors note that actual rates differ between types, so a scale change could remove the interaction.
agent_relevance: Overconfidence before solving is general. Predicted success is a poor stop-or-continue signal; use code-counted evidence.

source: Metcalfe & Wiebe (1987) Intuition in insight and noninsight problem solving, Memory & Cognition 15(3)
finding: A crowd statistic beat the person's own feeling. Normative difficulty (share of other subjects who solved each problem) predicted an individual's success far better than the person's own feeling of knowing, especially on insight problems.
numbers: Gamma with actual performance. Insight: normative .77 versus personal .08. Algebra: normative .60 versus personal .40. Own-versus-normative by problem-type interaction F(1,46)=10.13. Difficulty was computed on the same subjects (each contributes 2.1 percent), a small artificial inflation.
quote: noninsight problems were open to accurate predictions of performance, whereas insight problems were opaque to such predictions
limits: The authors argue a restricted-range explanation for the zero FOK is unlikely because normative gamma is high.
agent_relevance: Supports using external base rates (past solve rate on similar items, measured by code) instead of in-the-moment self-assessment. Matches G1 and the S6 note.

source: Metcalfe & Wiebe (1987) Intuition in insight and noninsight problem solving, Memory & Cognition 15(3)
finding: The authors proposed to define insight by the metacognitive pattern itself: a step-function warmth protocol marks an insight problem for that person. They also floated that this could track skill in a domain.
numbers: No numbers; proposal in the General Discussion, resting on the warmth gammas of .23 to .35.
quote: we propose that insight be defined in terms of the antecedent phenomenology that may be monitored by metacognitive assessments
limits: Circular if warmth is the only test. Later work (Hedne 2016, Laukkonen and Tangen 2018) finds warmth and self-reported insight do not agree.
agent_relevance: Defining insight by a felt step is a human-phenomenology criterion. The agent analogue is a code-observed jump (a check flips from fail to pass), not a rating.

source: Metcalfe (1986) Premonitions of insight predict impending error, JEP:LMC 12, 623-634 (as described in Metcalfe & Wiebe 1987 and Webb et al. 2016)
finding: Earlier warmth study: for correct answers warmth was flat then jumped; for wrong answers warmth rose incrementally. People sometimes gave an inelegant wrong answer with high warmth. A sudden feeling of nearness well before the answer tended to mark an error.
numbers: As reported in the 1987 text: on 78 percent of correctly solved problems and anagrams, warmth rose by no more than 1 point on a 10-point scale across the whole solving interval. Original paper not opened.
limits: Second-hand. The 1987 paper itself notes the incremental pattern for wrong answers may be due to a special decision strategy.
agent_relevance: Key danger signal: high felt closeness before a solution can accompany a wrong answer. Never treat expressed closeness as evidence; require a check.

source: Metcalfe (1986) Feeling of knowing in memory and problem solving, JEP:LMC 12, 288-294 (as described in Metcalfe & Wiebe 1987)
finding: Earlier finding that people overestimate their ability more on insight problems than on memory questions, and that feeling of knowing predicts memory retrieval but not insight solving.
numbers: No numbers recorded from the original. Metcalfe & Wiebe 1987 cite it as the source of the zero-FOK result they replicate.
limits: Not opened. Secondary description only.
agent_relevance: Memory self-knowledge is intact; problem-solving self-knowledge for novel hard items is not. Keep the two apart in any confidence use.

source: Hedne, Norman & Metcalfe (2016) Intuitive feelings of warmth and confidence in insight and noninsight problem solving of magic tricks, Frontiers in Psychology 7:1314
finding: Partial failed replication of the warmth result. With self-reported insight as the grouping variable, warmth did not differ between insight and noninsight solutions. Insight solutions were more accurate and more confident.
numbers: N=51 (8 more dropped for no Aha reports), 32 magic-trick videos of 15 s, 971 trials after exclusions; 29 percent reported insight. Accuracy .57 (n=281) vs .37 (n=690), t(506.9)=5.78, d=.51. Confidence 78.32 vs 68.95, d=.50. Differential warmth 2.92 vs 0.30, t(210)=0.79, p=.429, d=.12. Angular warmth .41 vs -.004, p=.266, d=.22. Including the last rating: 12.93 vs 11.65, p=.47.
limits: Warmth analysed only on 212 trials with 3 or more ratings. Magic tricks, not classic puzzles, and insight was self-labelled, so it is not an exact replication of the 1987 problem-type contrast.
agent_relevance: The step-shaped warmth signature does not follow the felt-insight label, so it cannot serve as the detector. Use code-detected impasse.

source: Hedne, Norman & Metcalfe (2016) Intuitive feelings of warmth and confidence in insight and noninsight problem solving of magic tricks, Frontiers in Psychology 7:1314
finding: Confidence tracked accuracy poorly for insight solutions: the area under the confidence ROC (Az) was at chance for insight trials and above chance for noninsight trials.
numbers: Az insight M=.56 vs noninsight M=.63 (33 participants with both, t(32)=1.06, p=.297, d=.30). Against 0.5: insight M=.57, t(33)=1.51, p=.142; noninsight M=.64, t(41)=5.43, p<.001, d=.82. Confidence higher for correct than incorrect: insight 81.34 vs 74.32 (d=.34); noninsight 74.31 vs 65.83 (d=.36).
quote: when a person solved with insight they seemed unable to judge whether they were right or wrong
limits: Az needs enough correct and incorrect trials per person so many people dropped; insight Az has a large SD (.28), and the two types did not differ significantly.
agent_relevance: Closest human match to our guardrail: when a solution comes with a sense of insight, people cannot tell if it is right. Verify such answers by check, not by confidence.

source: Hedne, Norman & Metcalfe (2016) Intuitive feelings of warmth and confidence in insight and noninsight problem solving of magic tricks, Frontiers in Psychology 7:1314
finding: Participants were more likely to repeat their incorrect solutions on a later recognition test when the solution had been labelled insight (perseveration after a wrong insight).
numbers: From the abstract: for insight trials participants were more likely to repeat incorrect solutions on a subsequent recognition test. Exact statistic not recorded.
limits: Only the abstract line was recorded for this item.
agent_relevance: Wrong answers that felt insightful resist correction. Supports G2: revise from located failing output, not from the model rereading its own confident answer.

source: Laukkonen & Tangen (2018) How to detect insight moments in problem solving experiments, Frontiers in Psychology 9:282
finding: Direct test of whether warmth-defined insight and self-reported insight agree. They do not at the problem level, though per-person counts correlate.
numbers: Of 631 correctly solved insight problems, 180 had 2 or more warmth ratings. Per-person counts: r=.61, n=51, p<.001. Per-problem: r=.08, n=182, p=.235. When warmth showed a sudden jump, 75.6 percent were self-reported insight; when warmth was gradual, 50.8 percent were still self-reported insight.
limits: Perspective article with a small experiment; only correct solutions with 2+ ratings used (about 29 percent of correct solutions).
agent_relevance: Two human definitions of insight disagree, so the felt step is not a clean marker. A code-defined impasse avoids this because it is behaviour, not report.

source: Laukkonen & Tangen (2018) How to detect insight moments in problem solving experiments, Frontiers in Psychology 9:282
finding: Argument against warmth as a detector: a gradual warmth pattern does not prove no insight occurred, because a solver can feel steady progress on a wrong strategy and then suddenly switch. Warmth data are also hard to analyse (they cite Weisberg 1992).
numbers: No new numbers beyond the contingency table; they recommend self-report Aha and a handgrip dynamometer measure.
quote: There is no a priori reason why an insight must occur without the feeling of progress
limits: Authors' argument, not a test of the competing explanation.
agent_relevance: A true restructure can follow an illusory progress feeling, so an agent tracking its own claimed progress will miss restructure moments; a code detector of repeated failure catches the stall.

source: Weisberg (1992) Metacognition and insight during problem solving: comment on Metcalfe, JEP:LMC 18, 426-431
finding: Published critique of the warmth method and its analysis. Known only through later citations; the comment was not retrieved.
numbers: No numbers. Laukkonen & Tangen (opened) cite it for difficulties in analysing and comparing warmth data.
limits: Not opened. Content known only through citations.
agent_relevance: Treat the 1987 warmth result as contested on method, not settled.

source: Chein, Weisberg, Streeter & Kwok (2010) Working memory and insight in the nine-dot problem, Memory & Cognition 38(7)
finding: A supportive replication of the warmth pattern on a classic insight task (hint-aided nine-dot). Solvers' warmth stayed flat for minutes, then rose in the last 15 s; non-solvers stayed flat.
numbers: Exp 3: 25 participants, 12 solved (48 percent) in 10 min, mean solve time 221 s (SD 136). Warmth scale -5 to +5 spoken every 15 s. Group by time interaction F(1,20)=20.60, p<.001. Solvers differ from non-solvers only at the last two ratings: t(20)=2.96, p=.007 at 15 s; t(15)=7.27, p<.001 at 0 s. Flat for over 3.5 min on average.
limits: Small sample (some solvers lack ratings; dfs of 4 and 9). Training problems and a hint used, so not the raw problem. Authors use it to validate insight status, not to test predictability.
agent_relevance: A close replication with the same flat-then-step shape. For stuck-then-solved problems the felt signal is uninformative until the end, so there is nothing usable to detect an approaching solution.

source: Chein, Weisberg, Streeter & Kwok (2010) Working memory and insight in the nine-dot problem, Memory & Cognition 38(7)
finding: Against the claim that insight problems use no planning: spatial working memory capacity predicted nine-dot solution, supporting the MacGregor lookahead model. Verbal WM did not.
numbers: n=54 (Exp 1). Spatial WM recall predicted solution: odds ratio 1.16, p=.004; verbal WM odds ratio 1.02, p=.52. Among 25 solvers: high spatial span solved faster, 264 s vs 367 s, t(23)=1.86, p=.038 one-tailed; verbal span not related (350 vs 282 s, p=.120).
limits: Correlational; one-tailed tests; nine-dot only. Earlier work (Lavric 2000, Fleck 2008, as cited there) found no WM role for other insight problems.
agent_relevance: Insight is not magic: the stuck state can come from limited lookahead, which wider search or explicit planning could relieve.

source: MacGregor, Ormerod & Chronicle (2001) Information processing and insight: a process model of performance on the nine-dot and related problems, JEP:LMC 27(1), 176-201 (Progress Monitoring Theory, later Criterion for Satisfactory Progress theory)
finding: Computational account of difficulty without a special insight process. Solvers pick moves that maximise progress (cover the most dots) with limited lookahead and monitor progress against a criterion (dots remaining relative to lines left). When no move meets the criterion ('criterion failure'), the problem space is widened to try novel moves. Impasse is a criterion check, not a feeling.
numbers: No numbers from the original (not opened). Chein et al. 2010 (opened) describe the maximisation plus lookahead model and test it; the criterion wording comes from search summaries.
limits: Not opened; description from Chein 2010 and search summaries. Evidence mostly nine-dot and variants.
agent_relevance: Closest model of our S6: impasse as a code-checkable criterion failure (no move improves the count), then widen the space. Matches the design where code, not the model, decides when to change operator.

source: Ohlsson (1992) Information-processing explanations of insight and related phenomena (representational change theory; as described in Chein et al. 2010)
finding: Restructuring arises as a response to impasse: impasse triggers spread of activation in semantic memory, which may activate a new way of approaching the problem and produce an Aha. Kershaw & Ohlsson (2004), cited in Chein, found nine-dot difficulty has several sources and large gains come only when aids address several at once.
numbers: No numbers recorded from the originals (not opened).
limits: Second-hand through Chein 2010. The theory has restructuring outside conscious control, so the person cannot see it coming.
agent_relevance: Explains the unpredictability of insight: the useful move depends on a representation not yet active. A reason to force varied operators (reframe, decompose) at impasse rather than wait for a feeling.

source: Webb, Little & Cropper (2016) Insight is not in the problem: investigating insight in problem solving across task types, Frontiers in Psychology 7:1424
finding: Three experiments with continuous ratings of Aha, confidence, impasse, surprise and pleasure on classic insight problems, non-insight problems and compound remote associates. Reported insight was higher on classic insight problems, but accuracy did not differ between insight and non-insight problems, and insight ratings tracked accuracy even on non-insight problems.
numbers: Aha means (Exp1 / Exp1a / Exp2): classic insight 45.16 / 49.25 / 42.47; non-insight 35.00 / 64.40 / 36.34; CRA 30.66 / 41.50 / 38.45. Accuracy: classic insight .51 / .49 / .45; non-insight .54 / .64 / .56; CRA .37 / .45 / .47. Insight minus non-insight Aha difference 10.15, BF10>150; accuracy difference insight vs non-insight 0.035, p=.81. Participant N not recorded here.
limits: Exp 1a and 2 filtered for English proficiency. Aha co-occurring with correctness cannot separate a feeling of rightness from an insight process.
agent_relevance: The label insight problem is weak: the same problem is solved with or without the feeling. Route by observed stalls, not by problem type.

source: Webb, Little & Cropper (2016) Insight is not in the problem: investigating insight in problem solving across task types, Frontiers in Psychology 7:1424
finding: The paper states the human discrepancy on whether sudden closeness marks right or wrong answers: Salvi et al. find insight answers more accurate, while Metcalfe (1986, p. 633) said feeling suddenly close often marks an incorrect solution.
numbers: No new figures for this point.
limits: Task and measure differences (binary vs continuous scale; CRA vs classic problems) are offered as the likely cause.
agent_relevance: The sign of the link between a felt jump and correctness depends on task; a rule built on the feeling would be unstable.

source: Danek & Wiley (2017) What about false insights? Deconstructing the Aha! experience along its multiple dimensions for correct and incorrect solutions separately, Frontiers in Psychology 7:2077
finding: False insights exist: wrong solutions often come with strong Aha. Correct solutions carry stronger Aha and are faster, but the distributions overlap.
numbers: 70 participants, 35 magic tricks, 2450 trials, 1778 with a proposed solution, 36.8 percent correct. Aha correct M=66.50 (SD 18.42) vs incorrect 52.34 (SD 18.78), t(69)=10.21. 37 percent (417 of 1124) of incorrect solutions got Aha above the mean for correct ones. Time: correct 35.81 s vs incorrect 42.46 s.
limits: Magic tricks, self-rated Aha, solutions rated afterward; may differ for classic puzzles.
agent_relevance: Direct measure of the cost of trusting the feeling: over a third of wrong answers feel as insightful as the average right answer. Matches the LLM false-aha pattern below.

source: Danek & Wiley (2017) What about false insights? Deconstructing the Aha! experience along its multiple dimensions for correct and incorrect solutions separately, Frontiers in Psychology 7:2077
finding: Aha is multi-part: Pleasure, Suddenness and Certainty are the main components for both correct and incorrect solutions. Relief marks correct ones and Surprise marks incorrect ones.
numbers: Mixed-effects models in Tables 4 and 6 (coefficients not recorded). Solutions n=1778.
limits: Component weights not copied from the tables.
agent_relevance: Certainty is part of the insight feeling itself, which is why self-stated certainty cannot validate an insight answer.

source: Salvi, Bricolo, Kounios, Bowden & Beeman (2016) Insight solutions are correct more often than analytic solutions, Thinking & Reasoning
finding: Counter-evidence: self-judged insight solutions on CRA problems were more accurate than analytic ones. Explained by all-or-nothing emergence: insight solvers time out rather than guess, analytic solvers guess prematurely.
numbers: Exp 1 (CRA), 38 participants: insight 93.7 percent correct vs analytic 78.3 percent, t(37)=5.66, d=.99. In the last 5 s of the window, analytic errors 29.4 percent vs insight 4.7 percent. 47.7 percent of problems answered, the rest timeouts. Same direction in all four experiments (CRA, visual, anagram and rebus).
limits: Self-labelled insight, short verbal-visual problems; conflicts with Metcalfe's classic puzzles and with Danek & Wiley's false insights.
agent_relevance: Confident sudden answers are right more often, but that is selection, not an ability to know. Pair with a code check anyway.

source: Chuderski, Jastrzebski, Kroczek, Kucwaj & Ociepka (2020) Metacognitive experience on Raven's matrices versus insight problems, Metacognition and Learning
finding: Rating the felt experience (Intuition, Suddenness, Pleasure, Certainty) after each item: on easy Raven matrices the experience matched insight problems; on hard matrices Suddenness and Certainty fell, like analytic problems. They describe the warmth method as the pioneer and note steady rise for analytic versus flat for insight.
numbers: 119 participants (online); four insight problems interleaved with Raven items. Exact effect sizes not recorded.
limits: Not about warmth directly; ratings are after each item. Felt suddenness varies with item difficulty, not item class.
agent_relevance: Felt suddenness depends on fluency, not problem class. Another reason not to read the model's sense of ease as a mode switch.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) Japanese children's riddles as a benchmark for machine insight and metacognition (NazoNazo), arXiv 2509.14704
finding: Benchmark built for LLM insight with a metacognition angle. 38 frontier LLMs on 201 insight riddles; reasoning models do better than non-reasoning ones but all are far below humans.
numbers: Non-reasoning models (n=16) average 7.60 percent, reasoning models (n=19) 17.59 percent, humans 52.9 percent (120-item subset). Mean difference 9.8 points, d=.946; logistic odds ratio for reasoning 2.29, 95% CI [1.99, 2.64]; population rates 9.42 vs 19.25 percent. Selected: DeepSeek-R1-0528 22.9, Gemini-2.5-flash-preview 10.9, Claude-opus-4 30.3, Grok-4 37.6 percent.
limits: Japanese single-answer riddles; thought-log analysis is qualitative and on a few models. The authors call the calibration observations hypothesis-generating.
agent_relevance: Insight-type items stay hard for reasoning LLMs, and the thought logs show the metacognition failure we should not trust.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) Japanese children's riddles as a benchmark for machine insight and metacognition (NazoNazo), arXiv 2509.14704
finding: Verification failure: models sometimes reached the correct answer in the reasoning log but did not endorse it and moved on, a failure of feeling of rightness. The authors say humans rarely do this.
numbers: Examples named: Grok-4 Q18, Q26, Q31, Q198; Claude-opus-4 Q35, Q135, Q179. No rate given in the passage read.
quote: models sometimes generated correct candidates but failed to endorse them
limits: Qualitative; frequency not quantified. The claim that the log reflects real intermediate reasoning is argued, not tested.
agent_relevance: A candidate was found but not accepted. In our design a code check, not the model's sense of rightness, accepts or rejects candidates (G2, G3).

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) Japanese children's riddles as a benchmark for machine insight and metacognition (NazoNazo), arXiv 2509.14704
finding: False Aha: models produced 'Oh! I've got it' expressions that ended in wrong answers; the model then rejected most of these ideas itself.
numbers: Claude-opus-4 'Oh! I just...' expressions occurred more than a hundred times; cases that led to a correct answer were rare. Grok-4 showed similar positive-realisation phrases.
limits: Phrase counts are for Claude-opus-4 only; no precision figure for the phrase as a predictor of correctness.
agent_relevance: An expressed Aha or 'wait' in a model trace is not a usable signal for correctness or for a switch.

source: d'Aliberti & Ribeiro (2026) The illusion of insight in reasoning models, arXiv 2601.00514
finding: Large test of whether LLM mid-trace Aha shifts help. They are rare and lower accuracy. Formal Aha events (earlier failures, stable earlier strategy, then a gain) are vanishingly rare.
numbers: 1M+ traces; GRPO-tuned Qwen2.5-1.5B (also 7B and Llama 3.1-8B). Shifts about 7.6 percent of Qwen-1.5B samples (6.31 percent pooled). Accuracy 2.57 percent with a shift vs 16.44 percent without, N=723,200. Formal detector fires on 1.79 percent. GPT-4o 0.88 to 2.21 percent shifts and DeepSeek-R1 0.00 to 0.25 percent across temperatures; GPT-4o accuracy lower with shifts at every temperature. More training did not help: marginal effects -0.0311 (crosswords, p=.027) and -0.0615 (math, p=1.6e-4).
limits: Shifts labelled by a GPT judge plus a lexical prefilter; small RL models in the main runs; crosswords, math and Rush Hour only. Selection effect: shifts occur on hard items.
agent_relevance: Direct support for dropping trace-level 'wait' cues as an insight signal. The model's own mid-trace pivot is a symptom of trouble, not a repair.

source: d'Aliberti & Ribeiro (2026) The illusion of insight in reasoning models, arXiv 2601.00514
finding: Reconsideration helps when triggered by an external uncertainty signal, not by the model's spontaneous shift. Appending a reconsideration cue, gated on token entropy (top 20 percent), raised accuracy where the model was uncertain.
numbers: Forced reconsideration (Table 5, paired): Math 0.3221 to 0.4062 (+8.41 pp; 50,574 wrong-to-right vs 23,500 right-to-wrong; N=320,000); crosswords +0.45 pp (N=83,200); Rush Hour +0.01 pp.
limits: Entropy needs token probabilities; gain is on math with a moderate base rate and negligible where the base rate is near zero.
agent_relevance: A code-computed uncertainty signal can trigger a rethink, matching G1 (doubt only on a signal). Supports an impasse detector built on measurable quantities, not self-report.

source: Wu et al. (2026) Aha moment revisited: are VLMs truly capable of self verification in inference-time scaling?, arXiv 2506.17417
finding: RL-tuned vision-language models rarely show an aha, and when they do it adds little. Self-verification with best-of-N did not beat simple majority voting.
numbers: Aha moments in 8.3 percent of responses (under 10 percent). Best-of-N with self-verification gave limited gain, with decreases up to -16.7 percent for the two VLAA models; majority vote gave steady gain (4.5 percent on GeoQA). Models verify the image poorly; self-verification sometimes better without the image.
limits: Vision-language models on geometry and MathVista; small models (2B to 7B).
agent_relevance: Self-verification is weak, as human self-monitoring on insight problems is weak. Prefer sampling and code checks to a self-judge (G4 caution on correlated votes still applies).

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language models (mostly) know what they know, arXiv 2207.05221
finding: Larger LMs are well calibrated on multiple-choice and true/false questions and can estimate P(True) of their own proposed answer. A trained P(IK) ('I know') predictor partly generalises across tasks but is poorly calibrated on new tasks.
numbers: 52B model used for the main plots; P(IK) calibration is worse out of distribution. Exact AUROC values not recorded (figures only).
limits: Calibration shown on well-formatted tasks. Insight-style puzzles are novel hard items where P(IK) calibration breaks.
agent_relevance: Contrast with the human result: calibrated self-evaluation exists in general, but is weaker on unusual items. Use only alongside an external check.

source: Ji-An, Xiong, Wilson, Mattar & Benna (2025) Language models are capable of metacognitive monitoring and control of their internal activations, arXiv 2505.13763
finding: Neurofeedback-style in-context test: LLMs can report and control some directions of their own activations, but only a small low-dimensional metacognitive space. Ability depends on number of examples, how interpretable the direction is, and the variance it explains.
numbers: No headline accuracy recorded; results are in figures. Reporting accuracy rises with number of in-context examples.
limits: Tests monitoring of activation axes, not progress on a problem. No insight task.
agent_relevance: Even when monitoring exists, it covers few directions, so a progress feeling in an LLM would be unlikely to be readable. Supports external instruments.
